steps: Decide which you need: percentage yield or atom economy.
Percentage yield: find the theoretical yield from moles and the mole ratio, then (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100.
Atom economy: (Mr of desired product ÷ Mr of all products) × 100, using every coefficient.
State the answer as a percentage; yield is never above 100%.
method_card.title: Yield and Atom Economy
method_card.content:
Two calculations, easy to confuse, so decide which the question wants first.

Percentage yield compares what you actually got with the most you could have made:

\[\% \text{ yield} = \frac{\text{actual}}{\text{theoretical}} \times 100\]

The theoretical yield comes from the limiting reactant using moles and the mole ratio. Yield is never above 100%.

Atom economy is a property of the balanced equation:

\[\% \text{ atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ desired product}}{M_r \text{ all products}} \times 100\]

One product means 100%; by-products lower it.

steps: Gold questions combine skills. For percentage yield, find the theoretical mass first (moles, ratio, Mr, mass), then compare with what was collected.
For atom economy, use every coefficient: 2Fe means \(2 \times M_r\), and put every product on the bottom.
For a limiting reactant, convert both reactant masses to moles and compare with the equation's ratio: the one in short supply runs out first.

steps: Spot which you need. Percentage yield: \(\frac{\text{actual}}{\text{theoretical}} \times 100\). Atom economy: \(\frac{M_r\text{ desired}}{M_r\text{ all products}} \times 100\).
The numbers are ready to use, so substitute straight in. For atom economy, add ALL the products on the bottom, not just the one you want. One product means 100%.
One calculation, one answer, given as a percentage.

steps: Now you are given a mass, not moles. Convert first: \(\text{moles} = \frac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\).

Use the equation's ratio to get moles of the product you want, then its mass with \(\text{mass} = \text{moles} \times M_r\). For atom economy, multiply each product's Mr by its coefficient before adding.
Put the theoretical mass into the yield formula, then check the value is sensible.

gold.display: Consider the industrial production of iron: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for Fe. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16, C = 12)

guided_steps.say: Atom economy uses coefficients. Desired is 2Fe; the other product is 3CO₂.

misconceptions.message: Use the coefficients: 2Fe = 112, 3CO₂ = 132, total 244, so atom economy = (112 ÷ 244) × 100 = 45.9%. Ignoring the coefficients (56 ÷ 100) gives 56%.
Sum all products with their coefficients: 2Fe (112) + 3CO₂ (132) = 244.

guided_steps.say: Atom economy = (Mr of the desired product ÷ Mr of ALL products) × 100. Both products form 1 : 1.

guided_steps.hint: Add the drug and the by-product.

guided_steps.done: 37.5% of the atoms are wasted as by-product. Atom economy = 62.5%.

misconceptions.message: Atom economy = (Mr desired ÷ Mr all products) × 100 = (250 ÷ 400) × 100 = 62.5%. Using the by-product (150 ÷ 400) gives 37.5%, the fraction wasted.

gold.display: Which reactant is the limiting reactant when 6.0 g of Mg reacts with 8.0 g of O₂? The equation is: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)
options: Mg, because it has the smaller mass
O₂, because it has the smaller mass
Mg, because the moles available are less than required by the mole ratio
O₂, because there is excess after the reaction

misconceptions.message: n(Mg) = 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25 mol. n(O₂) = 8 ÷ 32 = 0.25 mol. The ratio needed is 2 Mg : 1 O₂, so 0.25 mol O₂ would need 0.50 mol Mg but only 0.25 mol is present. Mg is limiting.
Compare actual moles with the equation ratio. 0.25 mol Mg needs only 0.125 mol O₂, so O₂ is in excess and Mg is the limiting reactant.

silver.display: Consider: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the atom economy for CO₂ as the desired product. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, H = 1)

guided_steps.say: Atom economy uses every product with its coefficient. Desired is CO₂; the products are CO₂ and 2H₂O.

guided_steps.done: 45% is lost as water. Atom economy = 55%.

silver.equation_hint: % atom economy = Mr(desired product) ÷ sum of Mr of ALL products × 100. For 1 CO₂ + 2 H₂O.

misconceptions.message: Multiply each product by its coefficient: 2H₂O = 36. Total = 44 + 36 = 80, so atom economy = (44 ÷ 80) × 100 = 55%. Forgetting to double the water (using 44 + 18 = 62) gives about 71%.
Sum every product Mr with its coefficient before dividing: CO₂ (44) + 2H₂O (36) = 80. Atom economy = (44 ÷ 80) × 100 = 55%.

silver.display: Ethanol can be made by fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for ethanol (C₂H₅OH). (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)

guided_steps.say: Atom economy uses coefficients. Desired is 2C₂H₅OH; the other product is 2CO₂. Mr of one ethanol is 46.

guided_steps.hint: Desired over total, times 100, to 1 d.p.

guided_steps.done: 48.9% is lost as CO₂. Atom economy = 51.1%.

silver.equation_hint: Total Mr of products = 2×Mr(C₂H₅OH) + 2×Mr(CO₂). Atom economy = 2×Mr(C₂H₅OH) ÷ total × 100.

misconceptions.message: Use coefficients: 2C₂H₅OH = 92, 2CO₂ = 88, total 180. Atom economy = (92 ÷ 180) × 100 = 51.1%. Using a single ethanol (46 ÷ 180) gives about 25.6%.
Multiply each Mr by its coefficient before summing: 2 × 46 = 92 for ethanol, 2 × 44 = 88 for CO₂.

silver.hint: One is about the equation's products; the other is about what you actually collected.
silver.display: In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, the atom economy is 100%. Yet the yield is only around 15% per pass. Explain the difference between atom economy and percentage yield in one sentence.
options: Atom economy measures what fraction of reactant atoms end up in the desired product; yield measures how much product was actually obtained compared with the maximum possible
Atom economy and yield are the same thing measured differently
Yield measures wasted atoms; atom economy measures how fast the reaction goes
Atom economy is only relevant in industry; yield applies to school experiments

misconceptions.message: Atom economy is about the reaction equation (types of products). Yield is about what you actually collect compared with the theoretical maximum.
